title: Activists Win Pause on Data Centres in Mississauga, but Questions Remain About Provincial Regulation
text:
Mississauga.ca

Mississauga "one of the first big cities to address this matter and push back against this data rush”

Activists in Mississauga scored a victory in the fight against unregulated data centres last week after city council voted unanimously to pause new large digital infrastructure projects for the next year.

But despite their win, advocates are saying the job is far from over.

On September 16, Mississauga city council voted to enact an interim control by-law (ICBL) to effectively freeze any new data centre project in the city with a peak-power demand above 10 megawatts for up to a year, which is enough energy to power 10,000 homes.

During this pause, the city says it will conduct a “comprehensive policy review for major digital infrastructure facilities.”

Martin Reid, the councillor for Ward 9, where the data centre would be located, told PressProgress that he was really happy to see the ICBL get approved.

“Putting development before planning is never a good idea,” said Reid. “I think we landed at a good place as one of the first big cities to address this matter and push back against this data rush.”

The Toronto suburb was set to host a new 220,000+ square foot, 40 megawatt data centre in its north end. A development application to create the two storey data centre was received by the city at the end of 2025.

The company behind the application, Prologis, is a real estate investment trust with a client roster that includes Amazon, Fedex, and Walmart.

A data centre is a facility that hosts the cloud. They are warehouses full of computers that store personal data from the internet and are integral for the internet and artificial intelligence to function.

There has been an international backlash to data centres for their impact on power grids, drinking water, and carbon emissions. Last year in Ireland, data centres used 22% of the country’s electricity.

Ashly Batista from No AI Mississauga– a grassroots volunteer-run organization against the data centre– told PressProgress that given the current lack of regulations there is no way to tell what company would be using the data centre Prologis built going forward.

“With a colocation data centre like the one Prologis hopes to build, ensuring digital sovereignty can be even more difficult — to my understanding, there is nothing the city can do to legally track which companies leave or enter as tenants once the data centre is built,” said Batista. “[It] could be a Canadian firm now, and an American firm in five years.”

The data centre proposed in Mississauga is a colocation centre, meaning Prologis would build the facility and rent it out to other firms.

A spokesperson from Prologis told PressProgress they were disappointed by the decision from city council, and highlighted the 1,600 potential jobs the data centre would bring. The spokesperson said that Prologis currently didn’t have a client set to use the data centre, but were in talks with a large Canadian company.

Prologis also provided a statement shared with other news organizations indicating the company is reviewing council’s decision and considering next steps. The statement noted the federal government recently recognized data centres as “critical infrastructure” and established new principles for their “responsible development,” which Prologis has signed.

Mississauga’s fight over data centres has been ongoing for months. Over 300 people attended a contentious town hall on June 25. On July 29, after several hours of statements from Prologis and activists, council approved a motion directing staff to prepare an ICBL to pause development on digital infrastructure projects for up to one year.

Before the vote on September 16, several councillors spoke with a dozen or so anti-data centre activists outside Mississauga city hall.

Councillors Martin Reid, Sue McFadden, Joe Horneck, Alvin Tedjo, and Dipika Damerla told activists what to expect from council proceedings: that they’d skip the deputations and get the interim control by-law passed.

City councillor and mayoral candidate Dipika Damerla congratulated the activists, calling this “their victory.”

The agenda item for the ICBL was pushed to the top of the council meeting, and unanimously passed. Activists filed out of the council chambers and debriefed with each other in the city hall foyer, sharing congratulations, talking about next steps and giving each other a chance to say what they couldn’t in council.

Although the activists were pleased with the decision to enact the ICBL, several in attendance were unhappy that they couldn’t say their piece about data centres.

“While we’re very happy about the interim control bylaw, obviously it’s fantastic, it is a bit unfortunate to see the way that our opinions and our voices weren’t allowed to be heard,” Batista said. “I don’t know anyone who didn’t have at least a little bit of disappointment about not speaking.”

Some activists pointed to the imminent municipal election on October 26 as a potential reason why council may have wanted to keep things as uncontroversial as possible.

Rahul Mehta, an activist with Sustainable Mississauga and council candidate for Ward 8, said that passing the by-law can’t be the end of the city listening to the public’s opinion on this issue.

“We want to see consultations, we want to see town halls, we want to see dialogue between different proponents,” said Mehta. “We don’t want this to be a vote that was expedited simply because it’s an election year.”

Councillor Reid said that the council thought by expediting the vote, they’d run less of a risk of having the ICBL not pass.

“In those deputations you [the residents] were saying ‘we want an ICBL,’ Wednesday was saying ‘we heard you’,” said Reid. “Let’s expedite this and get it done as quick as possible and get your desired outcome as fast as possible.”

The ICBL gives the city the time to research, develop and enact regulations for data centres to protect the well-being of people living in the communities where the centres are built. But questions remain about what role the provincial and federal governments will play in data centre development.

Doug Ford’s provincial government has repeatedly circumvented the authority of municipal governments, overruled the city of Toronto on multiple occasions, ripping out bike lanes in Toronto, and removed the city’s stake in Billy Bishop airport when it opposed expansion. Ford also threatened to use the notwithstanding clause to reverse an Ontario Superior Court decision on a Kitchener encampment if it wasn’t successfully appealed.

“What is going to be their role as they create their own frameworks and their own sets of rules and regulations?” Mehta asked. “Will they overrule each other? Will they sidestep some of the rules we have and say ours are no longer needed because theirs go on top?”

A pitch deck from the federal government for international investors detailing Canada’s artificial intelligence “ecosystem” obtained through an ATIP has also been circulated to activist groups. The deck refers to Canada as “an emerging data centre powerhouse” and “the foremost destination for new data centres.”

The province launched a data centre “playbook” on August 13, to “attract data centre investment, create jobs and deliver real benefits to host communities.” In a general committee meeting on September 9, Mississauga city planner Shaesta Hussen described the playbook as “very high level” and that it “lacks details.” Another staff member added that there needs to be clear guidelines from the province, as well as potential legislative changes to the Planning Act, to allow cities to regulate data centres.

“Whether cities want to regulate these is a second question as well,” the staff member said.

In the same meeting, Mississauga mayor Carolyn Parrish suggested that maybe the province should be in charge of regulating these data centres.

“I think somebody at Queen’s Park should be regulating this, rather than us, and give us very clear guidelines so that we don’t have false information circulating,” Parrish said.

Parrish added that given issues with tariffs the city would soon be under pressure to accept data centres, “whether we like it or not.”

In spite of the uncertainty, advocates recognize the victory accomplished in Mississauga. Over the course of the next year, the city will create regulations for data centres, in no small part because of relentless and consistent grassroots community organizing.

“We had councillors talk about the fact that the amount of people in seats filling the chambers was part of what influenced their decision during the first vote,” said Batista.

“So your voice definitely matters, try to use it when you’re allowed to.”
